source.version: Journal version of record: Technovation 138 (2024) 103123; received 14 December 2023, revised 1 October 2024, accepted 10 October 2024, available online 17 October 2024 (p. 1)
source.title_on_document: Revolution or inflated expectations? Exploring the impact of generative AI on ideation in a practical sustainability context

supplement.where: No supplement is referenced. The Appendix (Tables A1-A3, Figs. A1-A2, prompts) is inside this PDF, pp. 11-13.
supplement.holds: Not applicable. Arm means and SDs (Table A1) and Kruskal-Wallis tests are in the in-PDF Appendix. No standard errors are reported anywhere.

paper_design_summary: In a project with BSH Home Appliances, the authors produced 146 sustainable-packaging ideas under five conditions: three ChatGPT-4-only prompt conditions (AI, AI-AI refinement, WoS-AI with Web of Science topics), one 2-hour workshop of ten BSH experts working without AI (Experts), and the same ten experts after receiving the AI ideas as inspiration (AI-Experts). Five other BSH experts rated every idea on 5-point novelty, value, feasibility, and investability scales; the paper compares condition means and counts of top ideas (score above 3) with Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square tests. No assignment was randomized.

studies.label: AI-only ideas (AI, AI-AI, WoS-AI) versus expert workshop ideas (Experts)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned to people at random. Ideas came either from ChatGPT-4 prompts written by the researchers (no person used AI) or from BSH experts in a workshop without AI. The ten experts were split into two groups by department, and each group covered one subdomain.
assignment.quote: we quantitatively compared five different idea generation conditions to learn how they affect idea quality dimensions such as novelty, value, feasibility, and likelihood of investment
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2 Procedure; p. 5, Fig. 1 and condition descriptions 1)-5)

arms.name: AI
arms.description: Context-specific prompt fed into the ChatGPT-4 interface; 30 ideas (15 per subdomain).

arms.name: AI-AI
arms.description: ChatGPT-4 prompt that refines the AI ideas with SCAMPER-style substitute/combine/add instructions; 30 ideas.

arms.name: WoS-AI
arms.description: ChatGPT-4 prompt seeded with 92 themes condensed by topic modeling from 979 Web of Science articles; 30 ideas.

arms.name: Experts
arms.description: Ten BSH sustainable-packaging experts in a nominal-group ideation workshop (15 min alone, 15 min sharing, 15 min refining), two groups of five by subdomain, no AI; 30 ideas.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The 10 people are the workshop experts who generated the human ideas; 5 further BSH experts served only as raters.
participants.who: Ten sustainable-packaging experts from six BSH departments (8 male, 2 female), all based in Germany; ideas rated by five other BSH experts from different departments who had not attended the workshop
participants.quote: Ten sustainable packaging experts from six BSH departments (development, logistics, procurement, production, quality, and design) joined the workshop. The group consisted of eight male and two female participants

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (ChatGPT interface; authors also compared OpenAI API outputs at temperatures 0.7-0.9 and found no substantial differences)
ai_tool.how_used: Researchers prompted ChatGPT-4 directly to generate ideas; no participant used AI in this comparison (AI-only output versus human output).

task.description: Generate ideas for sustainable transport packaging of home appliances in two subdomains: material-based solutions (EPS-free, plastic-free, material reduction) and systemic solutions (recycling and reuse systems).
task.duration: Expert workshop: 2-hour session; idea writing about 15 min alone + 15 min sharing + 15 min refining

outcomes.name: Novelty rating ("The idea is original and disruptive")
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Five BSH experts rated each idea on a 5-point Likert scale. Reported as condition mean (SD) across ideas (Table A1) and as counts of top ideas (score above 3) versus expected counts (Fig. 2, chi-square test). Paper does not state how the five raters' scores were combined.

contrasts.reported: Mean novelty (SD): AI 3.13 (0.48), N=30; AI-AI 3.21 (0.63), N=30; WoS-AI 3.08 (0.58), N=30; Experts 2.73 (0.52), N=30 (N = ideas). Kruskal-Wallis across all five groups 13.568 (p = 0.009). Top novelty ideas: chi-square p = 0.015; text says 22 of 30 AI ideas particularly novel.
contrasts.locator: p. 11, Table A1; p. 6, Section 4.1 and Fig. 2

outcomes.name: Value rating ("The idea solves the problem of more sustainable packaging and creates environmental benefit")
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Five BSH expert raters, 5-point Likert. Means (SD) in Table A1; top-idea counts in Fig. 2.

contrasts.reported: Mean value (SD): AI 3.08 (0.65); AI-AI 2.86 (0.59); WoS-AI 2.81 (0.69); Experts 3.19 (0.69); N=30 ideas each. Kruskal-Wallis across five groups 11.127 (p = 0.025). Top value ideas: chi-square p = 0.266; text says 26 of 30 expert ideas particularly valuable and two thirds of AI ideas highly useful.
contrasts.locator: p. 11, Table A1; p. 6, Section 4.1 and Fig. 2

outcomes.name: Feasibility rating ("The idea is feasible within technological and long-term regulatory constraints and can be integrated into existing BSH processes")
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Five BSH expert raters, 5-point Likert. Means (SD) in Table A1; top-idea counts in Fig. 2.

contrasts.reported: Mean feasibility (SD): AI 2.39 (0.42); AI-AI 2.40 (0.52); WoS-AI 2.43 (0.51); Experts 2.81 (0.65); N=30 ideas each. Kruskal-Wallis across five groups 8.480 (p = 0.076). Top feasibility ideas: chi-square p = 0.078.
contrasts.locator: p. 11, Table A1; p. 6, Section 4.1 and Fig. 2

outcomes.name: Investability rating ("The long-term financial and business impact makes the idea worth investing in")
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Investability: rated likelihood the idea is worth investing in, five BSH expert raters, 5-point Likert. Means (SD) in Table A1; top-idea counts in Fig. 2.

contrasts.reported: Mean investability (SD): AI 2.51 (0.55); AI-AI 2.34 (0.51); WoS-AI 2.32 (0.61); Experts 2.78 (0.68); N=30 ideas each. Kruskal-Wallis across five groups 9.603 (p = 0.048). Top investability ideas: chi-square p = 0.203; 12 of 30 expert ideas were top ideas.
contrasts.locator: p. 11, Table A1; p. 6, Section 4.1 and Fig. 2

outcomes.name: Top novelty-and-value ideas ("highly innovative": novelty and value both above 3)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas scoring above 3 on both novelty and value, compared with expected count under a random distribution (chi-square). Further combinations (novelty/value/feasibility, novelty/value/investability, all four) showed no significant differences.

contrasts.reported: Chi-square across five groups p = 0.018. AI 13 of 30, AI-AI 13 of 30, Experts 11 of 30 highly innovative ideas; other combined dimensions: no statistically significant differences.

outcomes.name: Thematic diversity: number of topics per condition
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Ideas inductively coded by the authors into topic clusters and thematic aspects; number of distinct topics per condition (Table A3). Descriptive only.

contrasts.reported: Number of topics: AI 21; AI-AI 17; WoS-AI 21; Experts 13. No test reported.

diversity_detail.metric: Count of distinct hand-coded topics (thematic aspects) in each condition's idea pool
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each condition's whole pool of ideas (30 ideas per condition)
diversity_detail.notes: Compares AI output with human output, so it answers none of the three questions. Topic clusters were coded inductively by the authors; coding not always mutually exclusive.

studies.label: Same ten experts with AI-generated ideas as inspiration (AI-Experts) versus without (Experts)

assignment.what_was_assigned: All ten experts did both conditions in the workshop: first the Experts round without AI, then, after a long break, the AI-Experts round in which they received the AI condition's ideas as inspiration. Subdomains were swapped between rounds across the two groups. Order of conditions was fixed (Experts first); no randomization is described.
assignment.quote: the first group generated ideas in the material-based solutions subdomain described in the Experts condition, and then, after a long break, in the systemic solutions subdomain described in the AI–Experts condition. For the other group, the procedure was the other way round.

arms.name: AI-Experts
arms.description: Workshop experts received the AI-condition ideas as inspiration for their idea generation, on the other subdomain; 26 ideas.

arms.name: Experts
arms.description: Same workshop experts generating ideas without AI input (nominal group technique); 30 ideas.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The same 10 people appear in both arms (within-person).
participants.who: Ten BSH sustainable-packaging experts (8 male, 2 female) split into two groups of five, employees from the same department placed in different groups
participants.quote: We separated the participants into two groups, allocating employees from the same departments to different groups.

ai_tool.how_used: Experts received the 30 AI-generated ideas from the AI condition as inspiration before generating their own ideas; they did not interact with the model.

task.description: Sustainable packaging ideas for home appliances, material-based or systemic subdomain (swapped relative to the experts' first round).
task.duration: Within a 2-hour workshop; not stated separately for the AI-Experts round

outcomes.name: Novelty rating
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Five BSH expert raters, 5-point Likert ("original and disruptive"). Means (SD) across ideas in Table A1; top-idea counts in Fig. 2.

contrasts.reported: Mean novelty (SD): AI-Experts 2.91 (0.53), N=26; Experts 2.73 (0.52), N=30 (N = ideas). Kruskal-Wallis across all five groups 13.568 (p = 0.009); no pairwise test reported.
Mean value (SD): AI-Experts 2.72 (0.68), N=26; Experts 3.19 (0.69), N=30. Kruskal-Wallis across five groups 11.127 (p = 0.025).
Mean feasibility (SD): AI-Experts 2.35 (0.91), N=26; Experts 2.81 (0.65), N=30. Kruskal-Wallis across five groups 8.480 (p = 0.076).

outcomes.name: Investability rating
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Investability: rated worth of investing in the idea, five BSH expert raters, 5-point Likert.

contrasts.reported: Mean investability (SD): AI-Experts 2.40 (0.70), N=26; Experts 2.78 (0.68), N=30. Kruskal-Wallis across five groups 9.603 (p = 0.048).

outcomes.name: Top novelty-and-value ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas scoring above 3 on both novelty and value versus expected count (chi-square across five groups).

contrasts.reported: Chi-square across five groups p = 0.018. Experts 11 of 30 highly innovative ideas; experts exposed to AI-generated ideas "showed by far the worst performance" (Fig. 3 count about 2, read from figure).

outcomes.name: Thematic diversity: number of topics per condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Hand-coded distinct topics per condition (Table A3). Descriptive only.

contrasts.reported: Number of topics: AI-Experts 16; Experts 13. No test reported.

diversity_detail.metric: Count of distinct hand-coded topics in each condition's idea pool
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each condition's whole pool of ideas (26 AI-Experts ideas, 30 Experts ideas), pooled over the two expert groups
diversity_detail.notes: Pools differ in subdomain composition within each group; counts are of topics, not similarity between people.

company_involvement.description: Conducted in cooperation with and funded by BSH Home Appliances Group; ideators and raters are BSH employees; rating dimensions adapted with a BSH steering committee.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, title footnote; p. 10, Acknowledgements ("The research was funded by BSH Home Appliances Group."); p. 5, Section 3.2

eligibility.reason: The main comparison is ChatGPT-4 output versus ideas from a workshop of 10 BSH experts (AI vs human output). The only human-with-AI contrast (AI-Experts vs Experts) uses the same 10 experts in a fixed order (Experts first, AI-inspired round after a break) with no randomization, so it is quasi_people and far below 50 people. Outcomes are expert ratings of the ideas, so criterion 3 is met.

one_line_finding: ChatGPT-4-only ideas were rated more novel but less feasible than ideas from a 10-expert BSH workshop (mean novelty AI 3.13 vs Experts 2.73; feasibility 2.39 vs 2.81; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.009 and 0.076; Table A1, p. 11), and the same experts given AI ideas as inspiration produced ideas rated lower on value, feasibility, and investability.
open_questions: Fig. A1 (p. 11) shows six boxplot groups including an "Experts-AI" condition that Table A1, Fig. 1, and the text never describe; the appendix prompt heading also reads "AI-AI und Experts-AI". It is unclear whether a sixth condition existed or this is a labeling error.

Text on p. 6 says 22 of 30 AI ideas were particularly novel and 26 of 30 expert ideas particularly valuable, but the Fig. 2 dots read at about 20 and about 23. The audit should check these counts against the figure.
The paper does not say how the five raters' scores were combined per idea (mean or otherwise) before computing condition means and top-idea indicators.
notes: Total ideas = 146 (30+30+30+26+30). Tests are omnibus across all five conditions (Kruskal-Wallis on ratings, chi-square on top-idea counts); no pairwise contrasts or standard errors are reported, and all Ns in Table A1 are ideas, not people. Qualitative focus group (20 min) and next-day email survey of the 10 workshop experts (response rate 100%) are self-report and not coded. Data not shared: "The authors do not have permission to share data." (p. 13).
